title: Why Does an Octopus Have 3 Hearts? 🐙
description:
Why does an octopus have three hearts? Two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills, a third systemic heart sends it around the body, and because octopus blood carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin (which makes it blue), it needs that extra pumping power, while the body heart even stops beating when the octopus swims.

topic: Why does an octopus have three hearts?
script: Three hearts, blue blood, and you'd never guess why one octopus needs 3. Two of the hearts sit right by the gills. Their only job is pushing blood through them, so it can grab oxygen from the water. The third heart is the big one. It sends that fresh blood out to the whole body. So why not just one? Octopus blood carries oxygen with copper, not iron. That copper is what makes it blue, and it's worse at holding oxygen than ours. So the octopus needs extra pumping power. Now the weird part. When an octopus swims, that main body heart actually stops beating. Swimming tires it out fast, which is why octopuses would much rather crawl. If you had three hearts, what would you do with the spare one?
key_facts: Octopuses have three hearts: two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills, one systemic heart pumps it to the body
Octopus blood uses copper-based hemocyanin, which turns blue when oxygenated
Hemocyanin carries oxygen less efficiently than our iron-based hemoglobin
The systemic heart stops beating while the octopus swims, so octopuses prefer crawling
